dna-replication-s1.title: DNA density bands after a shift from heavy to light nitrogen
dna-replication-s1.html: Bacteria were grown for many generations in a medium whose only nitrogen was heavy 15N, then moved to a medium with ordinary light 14N. items.q: Which statement correctly describes the results for the blended samples?

items.q: Why were sulfur and phosphorus chosen as the two labels?
options: Proteins contain sulfur but almost no phosphorus; DNA contains phosphorus but no sulfur.
Sulfur labels the outside of a phage and phosphorus the inside, whatever molecules happen to be there.
Radioactive sulfur and phosphorus give off different colors, so the two can be told apart in one tube.
Both elements are found in DNA and in protein, so either label shows where the whole phage goes.

items.q: Even after blending, 18% of the <sup>35</sup>S was in the cell pellet. Which explanation is best supported by all the data?
options: Some empty coats stayed stuck to the cells; unblended samples show that coats stay on unless shaken off.
About a fifth of the phage protein entered the cells and then directed the making of the new phages.
Inside the cells, some <sup>35</sup>S was moved into DNA, so it stayed with the cell pellet.
Blending broke open some cells, releasing <sup>32</sup>P into the liquid and leaving <sup>35</sup>S behind.

items.q: Suppose the researchers had labeled phages with radioactive carbon (<sup>14</sup>C) instead. Why could that experiment not tell which molecule carries the phage's genes?
options: Both DNA and protein contain carbon, so label would sit in both the coats and the injected material.
Bacteria do not take up carbon from the broth, so the phages grown in them would not become labeled.
Radioactive carbon kills the bacteria, so no new phages would be released.
Carbon atoms move from protein into DNA during infection, so the label would end up in DNA.

items.q: Which conclusion does the last column (label recovered in new phages) best support?
options: The material the parent phage passes to its offspring is its DNA, not its protein coat.
New phages are built from the parent's coat protein, which is reused after infection.
The parent phage's DNA is broken down as soon as the cell starts to make new phages.
Phosphorus is used to build the coat proteins of the new phages.

They form a head at both ends of the embryo, because the Bicoid gradient becomes flat.
About half develop normally, those that inherit a working copy from the father.

items.q: How do totipotent and pluripotent stem cells differ?
options: Totipotent cells can form a whole organism, placenta included; pluripotent cells form any body cell but not placenta.
Pluripotent cells can form a whole organism, including the placenta; totipotent cells can form a few closely related cell types.
Totipotent cells are found in adult tissues, while pluripotent cells are found in the early embryo instead.
Totipotent cells divide by mitosis, while pluripotent cells divide by meiosis to make gametes.

items.q: A nucleus from a specialized tadpole intestine cell was put into an egg whose own nucleus had been destroyed. In some trials, the egg developed into a normal tadpole. What does this show?
options: The specialized cell still had a full set of genes, which the egg's cytoplasm switched back on.
Intestine cells keep just the genes for intestine, and the egg turned those into the other genes.
The tadpole's genes came from the egg's destroyed nucleus, which had repaired itself.
Specialization happens by losing genes, and the egg supplied the genes that were lost.

items.q: A drug blocks the proteasome, the protein complex that breaks down proteins tagged for destruction. Predict each quantity in dividing cells treated with the drug, compared with untreated cells.

variables.name: Amount of mitotic cyclin in cells an hour after they reach metaphase
Number of cells that complete mitosis and divide
Transcription rate of the cyclin gene

items.q: Pancreatic cells translate insulin as a single longer chain, proinsulin. Enzymes in the Golgi and secretory vesicles cut out a middle piece, leaving two chains joined by disulfide bonds; only this form is active. What kind of regulation is this?
options: Post-translational modification: the protein is changed after it is made
Post-transcriptional regulation, because the mRNA for insulin is spliced in the Golgi
Epigenetic regulation, because the insulin gene's histones are acetylated
Transcriptional regulation, because the insulin gene's enhancer is activated

items.q: In a fruit fly with an altered regulatory sequence, a Hox gene that normally works in the thorax is switched on in the head as well. The fly grows legs where its antennae should be. Which explanation is best?
options: The Hox gene's product is a transcription factor that switches on the leg program wherever it is active.
The Hox gene codes for a structural protein of legs, and now the head has enough of it to build legs.
Head cells contain leg genes that thorax cells lack, and the Hox gene moved those genes to the head.
The head cells divided faster than usual, and the extra cells became legs by chance.

items.q: In some vertebrate embryos, the optic cup (an outgrowth of the developing brain) normally touches the skin above it, which then forms a lens. When an optic cup is transplanted under skin on the side of the body, a lens forms there. When a thin filter that lets molecules through but not cells is placed between them, a lens still forms. What do these results show?
options: The optic cup releases signal molecules that induce nearby skin cells to switch on lens genes.
Lens cells are carried to the skin by the optic cup, and they divide to make the lens.
Skin cells everywhere form a lens on their own when the embryo reaches a certain age.
The optic cup has to touch the skin directly, through cell junctions, for a lens to be induced.

items.q: Which of these regulate gene expression after transcription has already happened? Select all that apply.
options: A microRNA pairing with an mRNA
Alternative splicing of a pre-mRNA
Acetylation of histones at a promoter
An activator binding an enhancer
Methylation of a promoter's DNA

items.q: Put these steps in order for a cell in an embryo that becomes a muscle cell.
options: A signal from neighboring tissue binds receptors on the cell.
The signaling pathway activates a master transcription factor in the cell.
The transcription factor binds enhancers of many muscle genes.
Muscle genes, such as myosin, are transcribed together.
The cell fills with contractile proteins and takes on a muscle cell's shape and job.

items.q: Which strain makes a polypeptide identical to the normal one?
options: Strain A
Strain B
Strain C
Strain D
Strain E

items.q: What polypeptide does strain D make, and what kind of mutation is it?
options: Met-Ala-Trp-Val-Leu-Asn-Gly: a missense mutation
Met-Ala-Trp-Glu-Leu-Asn-Gly: a silent mutation
Met-Ala-Trp: a nonsense mutation
Met-Ala-Trp-Val-Ser-Lys-Trp: a frameshift mutation

items.q: What polypeptide does strain A make?
options: Met-Ala-Gly-Asn
Met-Ala-Trp-Glu-Leu-Asn-Gly
Met-Ala-Glu-Leu-Asn-Gly
Met-Ala

items.q: Strain E gained three bases and strain A lost only one, yet strain E's polypeptide is far closer to normal. Why?
options: Three added bases add a codon and keep the frame; one lost base shifts each later codon.
Added bases are cut out of the mRNA by spliceosomes, but lost bases are not put back by the cell.
Insertions change just the DNA, while deletions also change the mRNA and the protein made from it.
A change near the start of an mRNA has a larger effect than one farther along, whatever its size.

items.q: How many amino acids are in the polypeptide made by strain C? Give a whole number.
Which claim is best supported by the colony counts?
options: Chemical Q causes mutations by itself; chemical P causes them after liver enzymes change it.
Chemical P causes mutations by itself; chemical Q causes them after liver enzymes change it.
Neither chemical causes mutations, because some revertant colonies appear on each plate.
The liver extract causes the mutations, and the chemicals simply help the cells to grow.

items.q: Why do the plates with solvent only still have about 22 revertant colonies?
options: Mutations also arise with no mutagen, from rare copying errors and everyday DNA damage.
The solvent itself is a weak mutagen, which caused a few of the spread cells to mutate.
Some cells sensed the lack of histidine and changed their gene so they could grow.
Some cells were contaminants from the air, carrying a working histidine gene.

items.q: What is the purpose of the plates with liver extract only?
options: To show that the extract by itself does not raise the mutation rate
To give the bacteria the histidine they need to form colonies
To show that chemical P needs liver enzymes to become a mutagen
To measure how many cells were spread on each of the plates

items.q: Chemicals that cause mutations in this bacterial test are treated as possible causes of cancer in people. Which reasoning supports this?
options: DNA is the same molecule in bacteria and people, and cancer starts from mutations in cell-cycle genes.
Bacteria and people share the histidine gene, so damage to that gene causes cancer in both of them.
Bacteria that mutate in the test have become cancer cells, so the chemical has already caused cancer.
The liver extract is human, so each chemical tested with it acts just as it would inside a person.

items.q: Which statement best describes the data?
options: Set 1's counts vary enormously, from 0 to 107, while set 2's stay from 13 to 26.
Set 1's counts are steady, while set 2's vary enormously from one plate to another.
Both sets give similar counts on each plate, close to the overall average of 17 colonies.
Set 1 has far more resistant colonies in total than set 2 has in total.

items.q: Which hypothesis do the data support, and why?
options: Hypothesis 2: an early mutation in one culture leaves many resistant descendants, spreading set 1's counts.
Hypothesis 1: each plate's phage turned a similar share of cells resistant, which explains the even counts of set 2.
Hypothesis 1: the cultures in set 1 met different amounts of phage, so their counts differed widely from one another.
Hypothesis 2: the cells in set 2 grew in one culture, so they could share their resistance with each other.

items.q: What is the mean number of resistant colonies per plate in set 1? Give one decimal place.
Why was set 2 needed?
options: It shows how much counts vary from sampling and plating alone, so technique cannot explain set 1.
It shows that cells grown in one large culture mutate more often than cells grown in small separate ones.
It provides the cells that are spread on the phage plates in set 1 of the experiment.
It shows that the phage on each plate was able to kill the normal, nonresistant cells.

items.q: In sickle cell disease, one base change replaces glutamic acid (charged) with valine (nonpolar) at position 6 of the β chain of hemoglobin. Which chain of effects explains the disease?
options: Nonpolar valine on the surface makes hemoglobin stick into fibers at low oxygen, bending red blood cells.
Valine changes the code for each later amino acid, so the β chain is shortened and hemoglobin fails to form.
Valine stops the hemoglobin gene from being transcribed, so red blood cells contain little hemoglobin.
Valine makes hemoglobin hold oxygen so tightly that little of it is released to the body's tissues.

items.q: A chromosome's genes are normally in the order A-B-C-D-E-F-G. In a mutant chromosome the order is A-B-E-D-C-F-G. What kind of change is this?
options: Inversion
Duplication
Deletion
Translocation

items.q: Which processes can move genes from one bacterium into another living bacterium? Select all that apply.
options: Transformation: taking up DNA from the surroundings
Transduction: a phage carrying bacterial DNA into a new host
Conjugation: passing DNA through a pilus between two cells
Binary fission: one cell dividing into two
Mitosis: dividing a nucleus into two
Spore formation: a cell walling itself off to survive

items.q: Most seedless watermelons are triploid (3n). Why are they nearly sterile?
options: Three homologs of each chromosome cannot split evenly in meiosis I, so most gametes are unbalanced.
Triploid plants make no meiotic cells, because the extra chromosomes block cell division in their flowers.
The extra set of chromosomes contains a mutation that destroys the genes for making seeds.
Triploid cells hold so much DNA that they fail to finish copying it during S phase, and so they stop dividing.

items.q: A student writes: "When bacteria are exposed to a drug, they mutate so that they can survive it." Which correction is best?
options: Mutations are random; the drug kills cells that lack a useful one, leaving cells that already had it.
The student is right, because the drug signals the cells to change the gene that the drug works on.
Bacteria are unable to mutate, because they have no nucleus to shield their DNA from the drug.
Mutations happen after exposure, but each cell mutates a different gene at random.

items.q: A pig cell is infected at the same time by a bird influenza virus and a human influenza virus. Influenza genomes are made of eight separate RNA segments. Which outcome is possible, and why?
options: New viruses with some bird and some human segments, because segments from both are packaged at random
New viruses that are exact copies of one parent, because just one virus can multiply in a cell
New viruses whose RNA is a single blend of the two genomes, because the segments are joined end to end
New viruses carrying pig genes, because the virus packages the host cell's chromosomes

items.q: A transposon (a DNA segment that can move within the genome) inserts itself into the middle of the coding sequence of a bacterial gene for an enzyme. Predict each quantity, compared with the cell before the insertion.

variables.name: Activity of the enzyme the gene codes for
Length of the DNA of that gene
Base sequence of a gene on the other side of the chromosome

items.q: The most common cystic fibrosis allele lacks three bases, so the CFTR channel protein is missing one amino acid out of 1,480 and the rest of its sequence is normal. Most of the protein never reaches the cell membrane. Which explanation is best?
options: The missing amino acid makes the protein fold wrongly, so quality control breaks it down.
Losing three bases shifts the reading frame, so each amino acid after the deletion is wrong.
The deletion removes the start codon, so the protein is made from a different starting point.
One amino acid out of 1,480 is too few to affect a protein, so the disease comes from another gene.

items.q: People who carry one sickle-cell allele are less likely to die of malaria. In regions where malaria is common, the allele is frequent; elsewhere it is rare. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Whether a mutation helps or harms depends on the environment the organism lives in.
The sickle-cell mutation was caused by malaria parasites, which changed the gene.
The sickle-cell mutation is harmful in each environment, so it should be rare everywhere.
People in malaria regions mutate more often, so the allele arises there more often.

items.q: How long is the plasmid, in base pairs? Give a whole number.
How many sites does enzyme B cut in the plasmid?
options: One
Two
Three
Four

items.q: Taking enzyme E's site as position 0 on the 6,000 bp circle, which map fits all three lanes?
options: B sites at 500 and 2,000
B sites at 1,000 and 2,500
B sites at 1,500 and 3,000
B sites at 2,000 and 3,500

items.q: Why does the 1,000 bp fragment in the last lane lie farther from the wells than the 3,500 bp fragment?
options: Smaller fragments slip through the gel's mesh more easily, so they move farther.
Smaller fragments carry more negative charge, so the positive electrode pulls them harder.
Smaller fragments are loaded into the wells later, so they start out lower in the gel.
Smaller fragments are heavier for each base pair, so they sink farther down into the gel.

items.q: A 900 bp gene, cut out with enzyme E, is inserted into the plasmid's E site. Predict the bands when the new plasmid is cut with enzyme E alone.
options: Two bands, at 6,000 bp and 900 bp
One band, at 6,900 bp
One band, at 6,000 bp
Three bands, at 6,000, 900 and 450 bp

items.q: At about which cycles do samples A and B first cross a glow of 20 units?
options: A at about cycle 18, B at about cycle 24
A at about cycle 24, B at about cycle 18
Both at about cycle 20, where the curves rise most steeply
A at about cycle 18, B at no cycle shown on the graph

items.q: Assume the target doubles every cycle. How many times more target DNA did sample A start with than sample B? Give a whole number.
Why do both curves level off near 100 units instead of doubling forever?
options: Primers and nucleotides run low and products pair with each other, so copying slows.
After about 20 cycles the polymerase denatures at 95 °C and stops working for good.
The target region is copied until it is longer than the dye can bind.
The dye starts glowing less once the DNA strands become double-stranded.

items.q: What does the no-template tube show?
options: The glow in A and B comes from copying target DNA, not from the reagents.
The primers are able to copy themselves into long DNA without any template present.
The virus is present in both patient samples, at the same starting amount.
The dye glows strongly in the absence of any DNA, so the readings need correcting.

items.q: Which conclusion is best supported by plates 2 and 4?
options: Some cells took up the plasmid, whose gene let them survive ampicillin.
Ampicillin causes the cells to take up plasmids that are in the medium around them.
Each cell exposed to the plasmid took it up, and each of them began to glow green.
The glow gene is needed for the cells to survive the ampicillin in the plate.

items.q: Plate 3 has a lawn that does not glow, though those cells were mixed with plasmid. Why?
options: Few cells took up the plasmid; without ampicillin, untransformed cells grew over them.
Cells do not express the glow gene unless ampicillin is present to switch the gene on.
The plasmid was destroyed by the nutrients on the plates that lacked ampicillin.
The lawn glows, but just after it has been exposed to ampicillin for a whole day.

items.q: Transformation efficiency is the number of transformed colonies per µg of plasmid spread on the plate. Calculate it for plate 4. Give a whole number.
What is the purpose of plate 1?
options: To show that the cells were alive and able to grow
To show that the plasmid on its own makes cells glow green on plain plates
To count how many cells took up the plasmid in the mixture
To show that ampicillin kills the cells that lack the plasmid

items.q: A gene and a plasmid are each cut with the same restriction enzyme, which leaves single-stranded sticky ends. Why can they then be joined into recombinant DNA?
options: Their sticky ends are complementary and pair; ligase then seals the backbones.
The enzyme recognizes the plasmid and attaches the gene to it once both are cut.
Cut DNA ends tend to join each other on their own, whichever enzymes made the cuts.
The gene's bases bond covalently to the plasmid's bases at the sticky ends without any help.

items.q: Put the steps of one PCR cycle in order, starting from double-stranded target DNA.
options: Heat to about 95 °C so the two strands separate.
Cool to about 55 °C so the primers pair with the ends of the target on each strand.
Warm to about 72 °C so Taq polymerase adds nucleotides to each primer's 3′ end.
Each original target molecule has become two double-stranded copies.

items.q: In Sanger sequencing of a short template, the new fragments that end in each base have these lengths: ending in A: 2 and 6; ending in C: 1 and 5; ending in G: 4 and 8; ending in T: 3 and 7. What is the sequence of the new strand, from its 5′ end?
options: 5′-CATGCATG-3′
5′-GTACGTAC-3′
5′-ACGTACGT-3′
5′-CTAGCTAG-3′

items.q: Researchers use CRISPR-Cas9 to switch off one gene in mouse cells. Which description of how it works is correct?
options: A guide RNA pairs with the target DNA, Cas9 cuts both strands, and faulty repair disrupts the gene.
Cas9 reads the codon table and removes the gene's start codon from its mRNA out in the cytoplasm.
The guide RNA is translated into a protein that blocks RNA polymerase at the gene's promoter.
Cas9 adds methyl groups along the whole length of the gene, so it is packed into heterochromatin.

items.q: To make human growth hormone in bacteria, researchers insert a DNA copy made from the hormone's mature mRNA, not the gene cut from a human chromosome. Predict what would happen if they used the chromosomal gene instead.
options: The introns would be transcribed too and, with no spliceosomes, no working hormone would be made.
The bacteria would make the hormone normally, since humans and bacteria share the genetic code.
The bacteria would splice out the introns but be unable to add a 5′ cap, so no hormone would form.
The bacteria would refuse to take up a plasmid containing human DNA, so no colonies would grow.

items.q: Which uses depend on PCR? Select all that apply.
options: Copying enough DNA from a single hair root to make a DNA profile
Testing a swab for a small amount of a virus's genetic material
Separating DNA fragments by size in an electric field
Cutting a plasmid open at a specific sequence
Joining a gene into a plasmid with ligase

items.q: DNA profiles compare the number of repeats at short tandem repeat (STR) sites. Why are STRs useful for telling people apart?
options: Repeat numbers at each site vary widely among people, so a match at many sites by chance is unlikely.
STRs lie inside the genes for proteins, so they differ between people as much as their appearance does.
STRs are found in some people but not in others, so their presence identifies a person.
STRs change in each of a person's cells as the person ages, so a profile shows both identity and age.

items.q: A patient with an inherited blood disorder receives gene therapy: some of her bone marrow stem cells are given a working copy of the gene and returned to her body. Will her future children inherit the working copy?
options: No: the change was made in body cells, not in the cells that make eggs.
Yes: a new gene placed in a person's body passes to each of her children.
Yes: blood cells carry genes to the ovaries, where they enter the eggs.
No: the working copy is lost from her treated cells within a few weeks.
